summary: EARTHSONIC is a scientific sonification platform that translates real NASA Earth measurements into sound, so anyone — including blind and low-vision users — can experience how our planet is changing. It pairs four NASA datasets (global temperature from GISTEMP, sea level from satellite altimetry, Arctic sea ice from NSIDC, and vegetation greenness from MODIS) with deterministic, documented audio generated in real time from the actual numbers. Every pitch, rhythm and tonal change has a scientific meaning: warmer years sound higher, faster sea-level rise sounds busier, less ice sounds lower, and greener land sounds richer. A Time Travel mode lets you select two periods, compare the measurements side by side, and hear the difference directly. The experience is fully accessible: every sound is described in plain words, every chart has a data table, and every control works from the keyboard. EARTHSONIC does not invent data or use random music — the same NASA measurements always produce exactly the same sound, with a fingerprint to prove it.
details:
What EARTHSONIC does

EARTHSONIC is a scientific sonification platform. It reads real NASA data files, maps the measurements to sound by documented scientific rules, and plays them back in a browser while showing the same data as a picture and a chart. The result is that you hear what the numbers mean — not a musical interpretation, but a direct, explainable translation of the science into sound.

How it works

Four NASA datasets are supported. For each one, the app reads the actual NASA file (not a copy of the values typed in), derives useful quantities such as warming rate and rate of sea-level rise, and applies a fixed mapping: pitch follows the main measurement, rhythm follows its rate of change, and tonal brightness follows magnitude as a second cue. The pitch scale is fixed for each physical quantity — it does not change when you select different dates — so two periods on the same scale are directly comparable by ear.

The Time Travel feature lets a user select two periods from the same record (for example, the 1990s versus the 2020s), compare them in numbers on a difference chart, and listen to the change in three ways: period A then period B; both simultaneously with A in the left ear and B in the right; or only the mathematical difference, where a voice rising above a reference tone means the later period was higher.

Every sound is described in plain words alongside the audio — the note name, the frequency in hertz, and the data value that produced it. This text is also read by screen readers. Playback can be downloaded as a WAV file.

Why it matters

Earth science data is overwhelmingly visual. EARTHSONIC makes it accessible to blind and low-vision users without removing any scientific meaning. It also reveals patterns that are hard to see: the accelerating rhythm of sea-level rise, the Arctic voice pulling ahead of the global voice in the temperature record, the busier bell pattern as record warm years come closer together. Sound adds a dimension that visualization alone cannot provide.

Tools and technologies

Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite 8, Tailwind CSS 4, Tone.js, Web Audio API. The core sound engine is pure TypeScript with no browser dependencies, so it is fully testable without audio hardware. 106 automated tests include an audio-frequency analyser that verifies the rendered pitch follows the data at low, middle and high values. No backend, no database, no paid services or APIs.

NASA data used

NASA GISS Surface Temperature Analysis (GISTEMP v4); NASA Sea Level Change Team GSFC Global Mean Sea Level (PO.DAAC); NSIDC Sea Ice Index Version 4 (G02135); MODIS/Terra MOD13Q1 NDVI via NASA ORNL DAAC web service; NASA Worldview / GIBS Snapshot API for imagery.

Scientific integrity

The app never invents or silently fills in measurements. Missing values produce silence and a text note. If data cannot load, the app says so clearly. Demo data, used for trying the controls, is labelled DEMO everywhere and never presented as NASA measurements. Every sonification shows a fingerprint: the same NASA data and settings always produce exactly the same notes and the same audio file, verifiably.

Accessibility

Built as a core requirement from the first line of code: full keyboard navigation, semantic landmarks, live text captions of what is sounding, every chart with a data table, high-contrast mode, reduced-motion support, and downloadable audio files so the experience does not depend on a live browser.
